summary: Momentum-preserving snapping for a ScrollRect: it glides, and the snap takes over once it slows.
overview: Add it beside a ScrollRect whose content is a layout group of evenly-sized items. Dragging behaves exactly like a normal ScrollRect; let go and it eases the nearest item to the centre of the viewport. Next/Previous buttons drag straight into its Inspector, and CurrentIndex tells you which item you are on at any moment.

WHO OWNS THE MOTION, which is half the tool. While you DRAG, and while the fling is still COASTING, the ScrollRect owns it completely — its inertia, deceleration and elastic bounce all run untouched. Only once the motion has settled does the snap take over, zeroing the ScrollRect's velocity so a single system is writing the position. The previous version snapped from the instant you let go, which is exactly when inertia should be starting, so the fling was overwritten before it could travel.
HOW IT WORKS — worth reading once, because the maths is the whole tool and it is also where every home-made snap goes wrong.

A ScrollRect does not have a concept of items. It exposes normalizedPosition: a 0-1 value describing how far along the SCROLLABLE RANGE you are, and the scrollable range is (content size − viewport size), NOT the content size. So an item's index has no direct relationship to a normalized position, and the tempting `index / (itemCount - 1)` is only ever correct when the viewport is exactly one item wide.

To CENTRE item i: take that item's centre measured from the content's leading edge, subtract half a viewport — that is what moves it from the edge to the middle — and divide by the scrollable range. To find which item you are ON: express the VIEWPORT's centre in the content's own coordinates and pick the item whose centre is nearest. Releasing a drag does the second, then the first, then eases there over a few frames.
useCases: A horizontal card or level picker that settles on one card.
A paged settings or tutorial strip with Next/Previous buttons.
Anything needing a 'page 3 of 7' readout — read CurrentIndex.
Pairing with PaginationDots, which binds to it in one call.

params.tuning: Match it to the ScrollRect's own enabled axis. Only that axis is ever written, so a two-axis ScrollRect keeps its other position when this snaps.

params.why: How quickly the scroll eases into the snapped position.
params.tuning: Higher is snappier. It is a lerp factor per second, so very high values arrive within a frame or two and effectively become a jump.

params.why: How fast a release must be to count as a flick.
params.tuning: Single Step mode only. Below it, the release is treated as a gentle let-go and coasts normally. Set it comfortably above Snap When Slower Than or the two rules overlap confusingly.

Momentum lets the flick travel its natural distance and the snap tidies up where it lands — a normal scroll view that happens to align, and a hard flick can cross many items. Single Step catches any flick above the threshold and advances exactly one step: the page-turn carousel feel, predictable but it overrides the physics. Switchable at runtime with SetFlickMode.

params.why: Also wait this long after the last input before snapping.
params.tuning: Exists for the MOUSE WHEEL, which moves the content directly and leaves no velocity to decay — so a speed test alone would be satisfied instantly and snap between wheel notches. A drag is unaffected in practice, because its velocity takes longer than this to decay anyway. Raise it if you spin the wheel in slow bursts.

params.why: The speed below which the snap takes over, in units per second.
params.tuning: This is the dial for the whole feel. LOWER and the scroll glides almost to a stop on its own, so the snap is a barely-visible final correction. HIGHER and it grabs control earlier and feels more decisive. Around 200 is a good starting point for a 100px item.

params.why: Optional. A Button that moves one step forward.
params.tuning: Drag any Button here and it is wired in Awake — no code and no demo-only glue. Leave it empty and call Next() yourself.

params.why: Optional. A Button that moves one step back.
How far one Next/Previous press travels.
params.tuning: Items moves a fixed number, set by Step Size. Page moves by however many WHOLE items currently fit in the viewport, so each press advances roughly one screenful and the count adapts if the viewport resizes.

params.why: Items per press, in Items mode.
params.tuning: This is the 'jump 5 places' number. Clamped to at least 1, so a stray 0 cannot silently freeze the buttons. Ignored entirely in Page mode, where the viewport decides.

params.why: Loop from the last item back to the first instead of stopping.
params.tuning: Off, Next at the end and Previous at the start simply clamp. On, they wrap — which suits a carousel and confuses a linear tutorial.

usage.codeNote: The content needs a Horizontal or Vertical Layout Group with evenly-sized items, and the ScrollRect's Viewport field must be assigned — left empty, ScrollRect falls back to guessing and the measurements have nothing reliable to measure against.

apiNotes.CurrentIndex: Which item you are on. Updated live WHILE you drag as well as on every snap, so a readout can simply poll it each frame rather than subscribing to anything.
apiNotes.GetNearestItemIndex(): The same question answered from scratch, with no stored state — the item whose centre is nearest the viewport's centre right now. This is what OnEndDrag uses to decide where to snap.
apiNotes.ComputeCenteredNormalizedPosition(int): The centring maths on its own, returned as a normalized scroll position. Public because it is the part worth reading to understand the tool, and because it is what the self-test asserts hand-derived pixel values against.
apiNotes.Next(): Moves forward by CurrentStepSize. Clamps at the last item unless Wrap Around is on.
apiNotes.CurrentStepSize(): How many items one press will actually move, including Page mode's answer for the viewport's current size. Useful for a label that says what the button will do.
apiNotes.SetStepMode(ScrollSnapStep, int): Changes the step behaviour at runtime — for a 'jump by page' toggle in an options menu.
apiNotes.OnSnapped: Fires when a snap BEGINS, with the index being snapped to — not when the easing finishes. Deliberate and depended upon: PaginationDots binds to it, and a dot that lit up only after the animation settled would feel broken.
apiNotes.ItemCount: The content's child count, for anything that wants the page count without reaching into the ScrollRect.
apiNotes.IsSettling: True while the ScrollRect still owns the motion and the snap is waiting its turn — useful to grey something out until the list has stopped.
apiNotes.SetFlickMode(ScrollSnapFlick): Swaps the flick behaviour at runtime, so the two feels can be compared without leaving Play mode.
apiNotes.FlickMode: The current flick behaviour, for a label that says which one is active.
apiNotes.ShouldHandOff(float, float, float, float: The handoff rule as one pure function: settled means slow enough AND quiet for long enough. Public and static so it is testable without a pointer, a frame loop or a real fling — none of which exist in batch mode.
apiNotes.FlickTargetIndex(int, float, int): Which item a flick lands on. Positive velocity means the CONTENT is moving forward along the axis, which reveals EARLIER items, so it goes to the previous one. Getting that sign backwards sends a flick precisely the wrong way, which is why it is pulled out and tested.
apiNotes.CurrentItem: The RectTransform you are actually on, not just its index — for when the answer is "read the data off the card I am looking at".
apiNotes.CurrentItemObject: The same thing as a GameObject, for GetComponent.
apiNotes.GetItem(int): Any index, not only the current one. Out of range returns null rather than throwing, because a list still being populated is a normal state rather than a bug at the call site.

gotchas.title: It measured every item half a width out — fixed, and this is why it looked broken
gotchas.body: The previous version computed an item's centre as `anchoredPosition + size * 0.5`, believing a layout group leaves anchoredPosition relative to the content's leading edge. It does not. A layout group positions children with SetInsetAndSizeFromParentEdge, which sets the child's ANCHOR to that edge and then sets anchoredPosition to `inset + size * pivot`. So at Unity's DEFAULT pivot of 0.5 — what every item built by the toolkit's own helpers has — anchoredPosition was ALREADY the centre, and adding another half size put every measurement half an item too far. Items landed half a width off-centre and the nearest-item search was biased the same way, so releasing a drag could select a neighbour of the item under the middle. It was only ever correct at a pivot of 0. Both measurements now transform a real point instead, which cannot be wrong about pivots, anchors or stretched rects.

gotchas.title: The mouse wheel snaps too now — it never used to
gotchas.body: The component only handled drags, so on desktop the wheel left the strip wherever it stopped. It now implements IScrollHandler as well. Both it and the ScrollRect receive the event, because the event system delivers to every handler on the GameObject, so nothing is forwarded and nothing is consumed.

gotchas.title: The elastic bounce is allowed to finish before the snap moves
gotchas.body: Overshooting past either end drives the normalized position outside 0..1, and while it is out there the snap deliberately waits — cutting the rubber-band short is exactly the feel the ScrollRect is there to provide. The visible consequence is that snapping at the very first or last item happens slightly later than in the middle of the list.

gotchas.title: Assign the ScrollRect's Viewport field
gotchas.body: Left empty, ScrollRect falls back to guessing which rect is the viewport, and every measurement here is taken against it. The component falls back to its own RectTransform, which is usually right but not always.

gotchas.title: The first and last items usually cannot be centred
gotchas.body: Not a bug — there is no scroll range left to put them in the middle with. They clamp to the ends of the range instead, which is what you want. It does mean that snapping to item 0 and then asking GetNearestItemIndex can legitimately answer 1.

gotchas.title: Page mode moves whole items, not exactly one viewport
gotchas.body: A viewport 3.4 items wide advances by 3. Advancing by 3.4 would land mid-item on every press, which defeats the point of snapping.

gotchas.title: Items must be evenly sized for Page mode
gotchas.body: It measures the FIRST item to work out how many fit. Mixed-size items make that number meaningless — use Items mode there.

gotchas.title: An index is a position, not an identity
gotchas.body: CurrentIndex and CurrentItem are both index-based, so inserting, removing or reordering the content makes a given index mean a different object. If you need something that survives that — saving which card the player was on, say — put your own component on each item and read it off CurrentItem, rather than remembering an index.
